blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this 2011 paper by Collobert et al. as a foundational work in natural language processing (NLP) that demonstrates how neural networks can achieve state-of-the-art performance across multiple NLP tasks without relying on task-specific hand-engineered features or linguistic knowledge. The authors introduce SENNA, a neural network architecture that performs well on part-of-speech tagging, chunking, named-entity recognition, and semantic-role labeling, often matching or exceeding traditional systems while being significantly more efficient in terms of speed and memory usage. The key insight is that neural networks can learn effective intermediate representations from large unlabeled datasets, reducing the need for expert-designed features. Colyer notes that while the paper predates modern word embeddings like word2vec or GloVe, it anticipates their benefits by implicitly learning semantic similarities between words through backpropagation.
paper_abstract: We propose a unified neural network architecture and learning algorithm that can be applied to various natural language processing tasks including: part-of-speech tagging, chunking, named entity recognition, and semantic role labeling. This versatility is achieved by trying to avoid task-specific engineering and therefore disregarding a lot of prior knowledge. Instead of exploiting man-made input features carefully optimized for each task, our system learns internal representations on the basis of vast amounts of mostly unlabeled training data. This work is then used as a basis for building a freely available tagging system with good performance and minimal computational requirements. ar Xi arXiv:1103.0398v1 [cs.LG] 2 Mar 2011 Google, New York, NY.
